conversation.content:
Hi there—I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Your Name], a clinician who specializes in helping new moms navigate the emotional ups and downs that can come after having a baby. Today I’d like to do a quick check-in using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually just called the EPDS. It’s a well-studied set of 10 questions that helps us see how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. Your answers are completely confidential, and my only goal is to understand how to support you best. We’ll go at your pace, and if anything feels hard to talk about, we can pause. Ready to start?  

First, I’m wondering: over the past seven days, have you still been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

I can still laugh sometimes—like when my husband does his goofy impressions—but I’ve noticed it takes more effort. A lot of the day I’m just so tired that even funny things feel kind of muted, like I have to remind myself to smile.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes, but not as easily as before the baby. A couple of times my partner cracked a joke and I surprised myself by actually giggling, yet other moments I hear the joke and just feel too worn-out to react.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do find myself looking forward to little things—like the short walk I take with the stroller each morning or that first quiet cup of coffee while she naps—but the excitement feels kind of dim, almost like it’s behind a fog. Before the baby, those same moments would light me up more; now it’s like I’m reminding myself, “This should feel fun,” instead of just feeling it right away.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that’s been happening. Yesterday she wouldn’t settle for her nap and I kept thinking, “I must be doing something wrong,” even though everyone says babies have off days. I know logically it’s not all on me, but I still catch myself replaying little moments and wondering if I missed some cue or held her the “wrong” way.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes my heart just starts racing out of nowhere—like I’ll be folding her tiny onesies and suddenly worry her breathing sounded different on the monitor. Nothing’s actually wrong, but I still feel this knot in my stomach until I go check on her again.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week I’ve gotten that sudden rush—like my chest tightens and I feel I need to sit down before I drop the baby. It’s only lasted a minute or two, and there’s no real danger, but in the moment it feels like something awful is about to happen even though I can’t name what.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes—some days everything feels like a pile-up. I’ll be trying to get her down for a nap and hear the dryer buzz, then the dog barks, and suddenly I’m near tears thinking I can’t keep up. I manage, but it feels like I’m barely treading water and any extra ripple makes me feel I might drown.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s not every night, but a few times this week I’ve laid down feeling okay and then my mind just starts spinning—worried I didn’t burp her long enough or that I missed a spot cleaning her umbilical stump. I’ll stare at the ceiling while the baby and my partner are both snoozing, and even when I finally drift off I wake up at the slightest sound.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do get waves of sadness, usually in the late afternoon when I’m running on empty. It’s not all day, but when it hits I feel kind of heavy and teary, like I’m mourning the “old me” even though I love my daughter. The feeling usually lifts after a shower or a short walk, but it keeps coming back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I haven’t actually cried much—maybe once or twice, and it was more like a few quiet tears while I rocked her at 3 a.m. Mostly I feel on the verge, but the tears don’t spill over; it’s like I’m too tired to let them out.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I might feel overwhelmed, but hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind. My biggest fear is not being well enough to take care of her, so self-harm feels like the opposite of what I want.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 17: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Post-partum mother, ≤ 3 mo post-delivery (per chart)  
Instrument: Edinburgh-based clinical interview  

<sym>Symptoms endorsed</sym>  
- Persistent low/“dim” mood, afternoon “waves” of sadness and tearfulness  
- Marked reduction in pleasure/reactivity (humor, outings, coffee)  
- Excessive self-blame and guilt over routine infant-care challenges  
- Recurrent, unprovoked anxiety (heart racing, “knot in stomach”)  
- Brief panic-equivalent episodes (chest tightness, fear of dropping baby)  
- Feeling overwhelmed and “near tears” when minor stressors accumulate  
- Initial and middle insomnia driven by intrusive worries about baby  
- No anhedonia remission; mood brightens only briefly after shower/walk  
- No self-harm ideation, intent, or plan  

<risk>Risk factors</risk>  
- Daily functional impairment (sleep, coping, emotional control)  
- Anxiety symptoms equal to or greater than depressive symptoms  
- Strong infant-focused vigilance with safety fears  
- Absence of suicidal ideation ↓ acute safety risk  

<screen>Screening observation</screen>  
Responses indicate clinically significant mixed depressive and anxiety symptoms consistent with <med>postpartum depression with anxious features</med>. Frequency ≥ 4 days per week, duration > 2 weeks. No psychotic, manic, or self-harm symptoms reported. Continue to formal EPDS scoring, rule-out medical contributors (thyroid, anemia), and consider expedited referral for evidence-based psychotherapy and/or medication evaluation.
